raw_text:
### Introduction
Transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) has revolutionized the management of severe, symptomatic aortic stenosis. Although transfemoral access remains the preferred route due to its lower mortality and vascular complication rates, approximately 10% to 15% of patients presenting for structural heart interventions possess calcified, tortuous, or narrow iliofemoral arteries that preclude standard transfemoral delivery [1, 2]. Historically, alternative approaches such as transapical, transaortic, or transaxillary access were used but carried significant surgical morbidity and prolonged recovery times [3, 4]. Transcaval access—defined as percutaneous entry from the inferior vena cava (IVC) into the abdominal aorta—was developed to circumvent these limitations by utilizing the retroperitoneal space and venous system for large-bore sheath delivery [5]. This review summarizes the transcaval approach, focusing on technical aspects, clinical evidence, complication profiles, and comparison with other alternative routes.

### Technical Planning and Procedure
Extensive pre-procedural planning using multidetector computed tomography (MDCT) and procedural simulation is paramount [6, 7, 27]. CT imaging identifies a calcium-free "window" on the abdominal aortic wall directly adjacent to the IVC, typically below the renal arteries and above the aortic bifurcation, while avoiding major collateral vessels [7, 8].

The procedure is performed under fluoroscopic guidance. A standard venous sheath is inserted in the femoral vein, and a directional catheter is advanced into the IVC facing the target aortic wall. Concurrently, a sizing catheter is placed in the abdominal aorta via a contralateral arterial line to act as a target [2]. A coronary guidewire, insulated inside a microcatheter, is "electrified" using a standard electrosurgical generator (cautery) to cross the cavo-aortic space [2, 9]. Once the wire enters the aorta, it is snared, and a stiff guidewire is advanced. This pathway allows the introduction of a large-bore sheath (up to 24 Fr) from the femoral vein directly into the abdominal aorta [10]. After completing the structural intervention (e.g., TAVR), the cavo-aortic tract is closed using a nitinol occluder, typically an Amplatzer Duct Occluder (ADO), deployed across the aortocaval tract [10, 11]. The pressure gradient drives blood from the aorta to the IVC rather than into the retroperitoneum, creating a temporary, hemodynamically benign aortocaval fistula that generally closes over time [1, 12].

### Clinical Applications and Evidence
While primarily developed for TAVR, transcaval access has been successfully adapted for endovascular aneurysm repair (EVAR) [13], mechanical circulatory support (MCS) [12], and transcatheter mitral valve replacement (TMVR) [28].

The landmark NIH-sponsored prospective registry evaluated 100 high-risk patients undergoing transcaval TAVR [3]. This study demonstrated a high rate of successful transcaval access and deployment (99%), with a 30-day survival rate of 96%. Major vascular complications occurred in 12% of patients, which compared favorably with historical surgical alternative accesses [3, 14]. A subsequent study by Lisko et al. analyzing the STS/ACC TVT Registry reported real-world outcomes of 228 patients, showing high technical success but highlighting the need for operator experience to minimize bleeding [15]. Long-term data from the NIH prospective registry at 12 months and beyond demonstrated that persistent aortocaval fistulas are common (around 24% at 30 days) but clinically benign, with most closing spontaneously by one year without intervention [30].

### Complications and Learning Curve
The most common complications of transcaval access are retroperitoneal bleeding, aortocaval fistula persistence, and aortic dissection [16, 17]. Standardized protocols using balloon occlusion, covered stents, or secondary occluders have mitigated catastrophic bleeding [17, 24]. Cost-effectiveness analyses suggest that despite the need for closure devices, transcaval access reduces intensive care unit and overall hospital stay compared to transapical and transaortic routes, offsetting procedural costs [18]. Performance improvements are associated with a learning curve; studies suggest that institutional proficiency is achieved after approximately 10 to 15 cases [23].

### Comparison with Other Alternative Accesses
Traditionally, transapical and transaortic accesses were the primary alternatives [19, 20]. However, these require thoracotomy or sternotomy and are associated with increased mortality and pulmonary complications [21, 22]. Transaxillary and transcarotid accesses have emerged as popular options; however, they carry a risk of stroke or brachial plexus injury [25, 26]. Transcaval access offers a fully percutaneous approach that avoids thoracic incisions and general anesthesia in many cases, facilitating rapid mobilization [29]. Recent comparative analyses suggest transcaval access results in lower 30-day mortality compared to transapical access, making it a highly viable option for patients with hostile chests or severe pulmonary disease [26, 29].

### Conclusion
Transcaval access is a safe and effective percutaneous alternative for patients undergoing large-bore structural heart interventions who lack viable transfemoral options. Advances in CT-based planning, standardized crossing techniques, and dedicated closure devices continue to refine this approach, establishing it as an essential tool in the structural heart interventionalist's armamentarium.
